title: Money Smart for Adults
summary: A modular financial education curriculum covering values, banking, income, expenses, spending plans, savings, credit, borrowing, housing, and more.
why_read: Use this as the backbone because it is broad, practical, and designed for people building confidence with everyday money decisions.

title: Your Money, Your Goals Toolkit
summary: A toolkit of fillable worksheets and handouts for cash flow, bills, debt, credit reports, goals, and money conversations.
why_read: Start here when the learner needs to turn broad advice into a concrete weekly or monthly money plan.

title: Personal Finance
summary: A free course with units on saving, budgeting, interest, debt, investing, retirement, income, housing, cars, taxes, college, and information safety.
why_read: Good for someone who wants short lessons and videos before reading denser reference material.

title: Credit Reports and Scores
summary: A plain-language hub for understanding credit reports, credit scores, errors, disputes, and related consumer rights.
why_read: A beginner should understand reports before chasing score hacks or paid credit products.

title: Understand Your Credit Score
summary: A focused explanation of where credit scores come from, why there are many scores, and how lenders use them.
why_read: Read after the broader credit hub to avoid oversimplified myths about a single universal score.

title: Introduction to Investing
summary: An SEC investor education page explaining major investment products and the fact that market investments can lose value.
why_read: It gives the right cautionary frame before a beginner moves from saving into investing.

title: Investing Basics
summary: A beginner investing guide covering securities, goals, risk, diversification, fees, performance, buying and selling, and volatility.
why_read: Use this to connect investing vocabulary to concrete decisions like time horizon, fees, and risk.

title: Asset Allocation and Diversification
summary: A focused guide to asset allocation, diversification, and rebalancing as tools for managing investment risk.
why_read: Read this once the learner knows the vocabulary and needs a simple mental model for portfolio risk.

title: Getting Started
summary: A community-maintained start page for personal finance planning, investing, and retirement planning with an emphasis on saving, diversification, simplicity, costs, taxes, and discipline.
why_read: Helpful after the official sources because it turns concepts into a low-cost, long-term investing philosophy.

title: Saving for Retirement
summary: An IRS hub for retirement saving basics, employer plans, contributions, fees, automatic enrollment, distributions, rollovers, and related tips.
why_read: Use it as a reference once the learner reaches workplace plans, IRAs, tax advantages, and retirement account rules.

title: FAQs about Savings Bonds
summary: A TreasuryDirect FAQ explaining the basics of Series EE and Series I savings bonds, purchase minimums, taxes, buying, and cashing.
why_read: Useful as an optional reference for safe savings instruments after emergency cash basics are covered.

title: Seven Secret Credit Hacks Banks Hate
summary: A listicle that pushes paid credit monitoring and high-fee reward cards while promising fast score jumps.
why_read: Rejected because it rewards shortcuts over understanding credit reports, repayment history, debt levels, and disputes.

title: Double Your Money in 90 Days
summary: A short video promising quick returns through concentrated options trades and leveraged crypto positions.
why_read: Rejected because the claims are speculative, unsuitable for a beginner reading list, and framed as guaranteed outcomes.

title: Budget Like a Millionaire Masterclass
summary: A paid course landing page with sparse sample content and heavy urgency copy.
why_read: Rejected because free government and nonprofit tools cover the same beginner ground more transparently.

title: Always Pay Off Every Debt Before Investing
summary: A heated thread arguing a single rule without considering interest rate, emergency savings, employer match, taxes, or personal risk.
why_read: Rejected as a primary pick because it is anecdotal and overconfident, although it could be a discussion example later.
